notes.meaning: King Josiah summoned all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem to meet with him. Even though God had warned that judgment was coming, the king was determined to lead his people in seeking the Lord. He knew that any true national return to God needed the support of the nation's leaders.

Josiah went up to the temple with priests, prophets, and crowds of ordinary citizens. The king personally read the entire newly discovered Book of the Covenant aloud so everyone could hear it. God's word was meant for every person in the land, from the greatest leader to the humblest citizen.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars think the book found in the temple was a form of Deuteronomy written not long before Josiah's time. Traditional commentators argue against this idea.

notes.meaning: Standing by the royal pillar, Josiah made a covenant, which is a sacred promise before God, pledging to obey the Lord's commands with his whole heart. All the people stood to join in the covenant alongside him. Josiah set the example, leading his people in an open pledge to follow God's law.

Josiah ordered the high priest and temple guards to clear out every object made for false gods like Baal and Asherah. He burned these idolatrous items outside Jerusalem in the Kidron Valley and sent the ashes to Bethel. Carrying the ashes to Bethel defiled that ancient centre of northern idol worship forever.

The king removed the unlawful priests whom past kings of Judah had appointed to burn incense at outdoor shrines. These men had offered sacrifices to Baal, the sun, the moon, and the stars. Josiah recognized that real reform meant removing the leaders who encouraged sin, not just destroying the idols.

Josiah brought the wooden Asherah pole out of the Lord's temple and burned it in the Kidron Valley. He ground it down into dust and scattered the powder over the graves of common people. By throwing the dust on unclean graves, he showed complete contempt for the false goddess.

Josiah tore down the living quarters of the shrine prostitutes that had been set up inside the temple itself. In those same rooms, women had been weaving hangings to honour the idol Asherah. Wicked kings had allowed shameful pagan rituals to corrupt God's holy dwelling place.

Josiah brought all the local priests out of Judah's towns and desecrated the high places where they burned incense, from Geba in the north to Beersheba in the south. He also smashed the altars built near the entrance of the city governor's gate. This stopped the scattered, unlawful worship that had spread throughout the land.

The priests who had run those local shrines were not allowed to serve at the temple altar in Jerusalem. Even so, they were still permitted to eat the unleavened priestly food provided for their families. God showed mercy by meeting their physical needs while still holding them accountable for forbidden worship.

Josiah ruined Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom so no one could ever sacrifice their children in the fire to the god Molech again. In past years, people had beaten drums there so parents could not hear their burning children scream. The king turned this terrible spot into a filthy garbage dump.

Josiah removed the horses that past kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun god, which were kept near the temple entrance. He also set fire to the chariots dedicated to the sun. Heathen nations believed the sun rode across the sky in a horse-drawn chariot, but Josiah completely removed this solar cult.

The king tore down the altars built on the palace roof and those Manasseh had set up in the temple courtyards. He smashed them to pieces and dumped the dust into the Kidron Valley. He destroyed these rooftop shrines to end all star worship once and for all.

Josiah defiled the pagan shrines east of Jerusalem on the Mount of Olives, which was nicknamed the Mount of Corruption. King Solomon had first built these shrines centuries earlier to please his foreign wives who served Ashtoreth, Chemosh, and Milcom. Josiah wanted no reminder of ancient idolatry left standing near the city.

Josiah smashed the sacred stone pillars, chopped down the wooden Asherah poles, and covered the ground with human bones. Under God's law, touching human bones made a person or place ritually unclean. Spreading bones over the sites made them forever unfit for pagan worship.

Josiah travelled north to Bethel and tore down the ancient altar set up by Jeroboam, who had first led northern Israel into sin. He burned the shrine, ground it to fine powder, and burned the Asherah pole. He wiped out the very birthplace of northern Israel's rebellion against the Lord.

Looking around the hillside at Bethel, Josiah noticed tombs and ordered the bones dug up and burned on the altar to defile it. This action fulfilled an exact prophecy delivered three hundred years earlier by an unnamed prophet from Judah. God's promises and warnings always come true, no matter how much time passes.

Josiah noticed a grave marker and asked the local men about it. They explained that it marked the tomb of the man of God who had predicted centuries earlier what Josiah would do to Bethel's altar. The king saw clear evidence of how God's truth had outlived generations of false religion.

The king commanded that the prophet's tomb be left alone so his bones would remain undisturbed. Because of this order, the bones of an older prophet from Samaria buried with him were spared as well. Josiah showed deep respect for a true messenger of God who had spoken the truth long before.

Josiah travelled throughout the towns of Samaria, tearing down all the shrine temples that Israel's past kings had built to provoke the Lord. Because the northern kingdom had collapsed, Josiah was able to use his royal authority to purge idolatry beyond Judah's borders. He worked boldly to remove everything that offended God across the entire land.

Josiah executed all the priests of those pagan high places on their own altars and burned human bones on the ruins before returning to Jerusalem. These men had led the northern people into total spiritual ruin, and God's law demanded their execution. Josiah fully cleansed the land of idolatrous leadership.

Josiah commanded all the people to celebrate the Passover to the Lord, just as written in the newly found Book of the Covenant. The Passover was the annual feast remembering how God had rescued Israel from slavery in Egypt. After tearing down false worship, the king made sure to restore true, biblical worship.

No Passover had been kept with such care, exactness, and devotion since the era of Israel's judges. Past kings had either neglected the feast or failed to follow God's precise instructions for celebrating it. Josiah’s Passover was remarkable because the whole nation followed God's written word with sincere dedication.

This grand Passover was celebrated in Jerusalem during the eighteenth year of King Josiah’s reign. It happened during the very same year that the Book of the Law had been discovered in the temple. Rediscovering God's word brought immediate obedience and great joy to the nation.

Josiah outlawed mediums, fortune-tellers, household idols, and all the detestable occult practices across Judah. He did this to obey the direct commands written in the law scroll that Hilkiah had found in the temple. He attacked hidden, private sins just as vigorously as he had torn down public altars.

Scripture honors Josiah by saying no king before or after him turned to the Lord with all his heart, soul, and strength quite like he did. He shaped every part of his life and kingdom by the Law of Moses. His reign stands as an unmatched model of wholehearted devotion to God.

Despite Josiah’s great work, the Lord's burning anger against Judah did not turn away because of the terrible sins Manasseh had committed. Josiah was deeply sincere, but most of the people had only complied on the outside while still loving their idols in secret. Even a godly king cannot change a nation whose heart refuses to repent.

The Lord declared that He would banish Judah from His presence just as He had cast out northern Israel. He decided to abandon Jerusalem, the city He had chosen, and the temple where He placed His name. Persistent rebellion meant that judgment and exile, which means being forced from one's homeland, were now unavoidable.

The rest of Josiah's deeds and accomplishments were recorded in the royal chronicles of the kings of Judah. His courage in tearing down idols and his devotion to God's law were carefully preserved in history. God ensures that faithful service is never forgotten.

Near the end of Josiah's reign, Pharaoh Neco of Egypt marched toward the Euphrates River to aid the king of Assyria. King Josiah rode out to intercept him, but Neco killed Josiah in battle at Megiddo. The righteous king lost his life in a conflict that was not his to fight.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think Kings and Chronicles preserve two different accounts. Kings may describe Josiah being killed at a meeting with Neco, while Chronicles says he was wounded in battle.

notes.meaning: Josiah's servants brought his body back from Megiddo in a chariot and buried him in Jerusalem. The people of the land then took his son Jehoahaz, anointed him, and crowned him king. The entire nation grieved deeply over the sudden death of their godly ruler.

Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, but his reign in Jerusalem lasted only three months. His mother was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah. His brief time on the throne began the final downward slide for the kingdom of Judah.

Jehoahaz did what was evil in the sight of the Lord, copying the wicked kings before him rather than his godly father. As soon as Josiah was gone, the nation quickly turned back to its old corrupt habits. Having a faithful parent does not guarantee that a child will walk with God.

Pharaoh Neco put Jehoahaz in chains at Riblah in Syria so he could no longer rule over Jerusalem. Neco also demanded that Judah pay a heavy fine of silver and gold. Judah lost its freedom and became a subject nation under Egypt's control.

Pharaoh Neco placed Josiah’s older son Eliakim on the throne and changed his name to Jehoiakim. Neco took Jehoahaz away to Egypt as a prisoner, where he eventually died. Renaming a ruler was an ancient custom meant to show that the conqueror held complete power over his subject.

Jehoiakim paid the heavy tribute of gold and silver to Pharaoh Neco. To gather this wealth, he placed a harsh tax on the people of the land according to each family's property. Rather than caring for his subjects, the new king burdened them to satisfy a foreign ruler.

Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother’s name was Zebidah daughter of Pedaiah from Rumah. His reign brought oppression, heavy taxes, and spiritual decline to the nation.

Jehoiakim did evil in the sight of the Lord, following the corrupt ways of past kings instead of Josiah's devotion. He rebelled against God's word, mistreated his people, and silenced God's prophets. Under his wicked leadership, Judah was pushed closer to total destruction.
